MUJAHID:v2p435/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p435/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v2p435/r1.claim: Mujahid says the ones to ask for a count are the angels.

MUQATIL:23:112-116/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:23:112-116/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:23:112-116/r2.claim: They say a day or part of a day, thinking their grave stay was only that long; the counters are the angel of death and his assistants.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p419#2/r2.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p419#2/r2.speaker: author
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p419#2/r2.claim: They answer that it was a day or part of a day because their worldly life now seems so small.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p419#2/r3.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p419#2/r3.speaker: مجاهد
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p419#2/r3.claim: Mujāhid identifies the people to ask about the count as the angels; Qatāda instead says they are the calculators who counted people's lifespans in breaths.

FARRA:v2p243/r4.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v2p243/r4.speaker: author
FARRA:v2p243/r4.claim: They say they do not know whether they stayed one day or part of a day, and are told to ask the record keepers, the عدون.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p49#2/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p49#2/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p49#2/r1.claim: Qatada glosses the command to ask the counters as asking the calculators.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p300#4/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p300#4/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p300#4/r1.claim: Al-ʿāddīn means the people who count or calculate.

TAB-FULL:v17p129/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p129/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v17p129/r1.claim: Most Medinan, Basran, and some Kufan readers take “he said” as a report: God asks the people of Hell how long they stayed, and they say a day or part of one because punishment makes worldly time seem short.

TAB-FULL:v17p129/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p129/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v17p129/r2.claim: Most Kufan readers instead read an imperative, “say,” reflecting their codex spelling without the alif; other codices have the alif.

TAB-FULL:v17p129/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p129/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v17p129/r3.claim: The declarative reading is preferable: the surrounding address is plural, so a command would naturally be plural “say”; singular “say” is possible, but declarative singular is more fluent Arabic.

TAB-FULL:v17p129/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p129/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v17p129/r4.claim: On the preferred reading, the people answer that they stayed only a day or part of one and ask the counters, because they have forgotten the duration.

TAB-FULL:v17p129/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p129/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v17p129/r5.claim: One explanation begins the counters' identity as the angels who record deeds and count people's hours.

TAB-FULL:v17p131/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p131/r1.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v17p131/r1.claim: Mujahid identifies the counters as angels.

TAB-FULL:v17p131/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p131/r2.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v17p131/r2.claim: Qatada identifies the counters as accountants or people who calculate.

TAB-FULL:v17p131/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p131/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v17p131/r3.claim: The counters are whoever counts months, years, and other quantities; they may be angels, humans, or others, since no proof singles out one group.

ZAJJAJ:v4p24#2/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v4p24#2/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v4p24#2/r3.claim: لبثنا is reported with two readings; العادين means angels who kept count of their stay.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p448/r5.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p448/r5.speaker: ابن كثير في رواية البزي
IBNMUJAHID:v1p448/r5.claim: Al-Bazzī transmits Ibn Kathīr's imperative قل كم لبثتم and indicative قل إن لبثتم, without assimilating the thāʾ in لبثتم.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p448/r6.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p448/r6.speaker: قنبل عن النبال عن أصحابه عن ابن كثير
IBNMUJAHID:v1p448/r6.claim: Qunbul's transmission has قل in both positions without alif.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p448/r7.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p448/r7.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
IBNMUJAHID:v1p448/r7.claim: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī use the imperative in both positions and assimilate the thāʾ in لبثتم.

IBNMUJAHID:v1p448/r8.author: Ibn Mujāhid
IBNMUJAHID:v1p448/r8.speaker: نافع وأبو عمرو وعاصم وابن عامر
IBNMUJAHID:v1p448/r8.claim: These readers use the alif form in both positions as indicative statements.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2511#2/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2511#2/r1.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2511#2/r1.claim: A report says God asks the people of Hell how long they lived on earth; they answer a day or part of one, and God calls their earthly life a bad trade for his wrath and fire.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2511#2/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2511#2/r2.speaker: عكرمة
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2511#2/r2.claim: “Ask those who count” means ask the people who calculate.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2511#2/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2511#2/r3.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2511#2/r3.claim: “Ask those who count” means ask the calculators.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2511#2/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2511#2/r4.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2511#2/r4.claim: “Ask those who count” means ask the angels; al-Rabi ibn Anas is also reported to agree.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2511/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2511/r1.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2511/r1.claim: A report says God asks the people of Paradise how long they lived on earth; they answer a day or part of one, and God calls it a good trade for his mercy, approval, and Paradise. He asks the people of Hell likewise and calls their earthly life a bad trade for his wrath and fire.

NAHHAS:v3p123/r12.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p123/r12.speaker: مجاهد
NAHHAS:v3p123/r12.claim: He says the ‘reckoners’ are angels because they count the duration.

NAHHAS:v3p123/r13.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p123/r13.speaker: الأعمش
NAHHAS:v3p123/r13.claim: He reads ‘a number of years’; ʿadadan is an explanatory accusative in both readings, and kam is governed by libithtum.

NAHHAS:v3p123/r7.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p123/r7.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v3p123/r7.claim: The two questions ‘how long did you remain?’ have different senses and neither is better; ʿadada sinīn has a sound masculine plural accusative, though some Arabs use a genitive with tanwīn.

NAHHAS:v3p123/r8.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p123/r8.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v3p123/r8.claim: This answer does not deny punishment in the grave, since a period of quiet must precede resurrection.

THALABI:v7p59/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p59/r5.speaker: قتادة
THALABI:v7p59/r5.claim: He interprets العادين as the people who count.

THALABI:v7p59/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p59/r6.speaker: مجاهد
THALABI:v7p59/r6.claim: He identifies the counters as angels who preserve and enumerate human deeds.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says God made them forget the punishment they had been undergoing.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r10.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r10.claim: The reading قل is an imperative to the questioner, not to the disbeliever, as the author explained for the preceding verse; Ibn Kathir distinguishes قل there from قال here.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r2.speaker: مقاتل
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r2.claim: Muqatil says they considered their stay in the graves to have been only a day or part of a day.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r3.speaker: المفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r3.claim: The exegetes say the severity of their punishment made them forget how long they had lived in the world.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas explains العادين as people who know how to calculate.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r5.speaker: قتادة ومقاتل
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r5.claim: Qatada and Muqatil take the command to mean asking the people who calculate.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r6.speaker: مجاهد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r6.claim: Mujahid identifies the people to ask as the angels.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r7.speaker: مقاتل
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r7.claim: Muqatil specifies the angel of death and his attendants.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r8.speaker: الكلبي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r8.claim: Al-Kalbi says they are the angels who were with the people in worldly life.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r9.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p83/r9.claim: The speaker of قال may be God or the one who asked how long they remained.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:23:110-113/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:23:110-113/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:23:110-113/r4.claim: They say a day or part of a day because punishment was lifted between the two blasts and they forgot their suffering.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:23:110-113/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:23:110-113/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:23:110-113/r5.claim: They tell the questioner to ask the angels who counted their time.

JISHUMI:v7p5098/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v7p5098/r4.speaker: ابن كثير
JISHUMI:v7p5098/r4.claim: Ibn Kathir reads قل كم لبثتم as a command and قال إن لبثتم as a statement, which suits the second as an answer.

JISHUMI:v7p5098/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v7p5098/r5.speaker: حمزة، الكسائي
JISHUMI:v7p5098/r5.claim: Hamza and al-Kisa'i read both verbs as commands, matching Kufa codices; other codices and readers use indicative forms, with قل addressed to the singular Prophet as a collective command.

JISHUMI:v7p5098/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v7p5098/r6.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v7p5098/r6.claim: Sukhr is mockery; nisyān means the opposite of remembering and also leaving something, with the latter closer to its sense here; labth and mukth mean remaining over time.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p432/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p432/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p432/r2.claim: The question concerns years in this world and graves; torment makes them forget the duration, so they answer a day or part of a day.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p432/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p432/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p432/r3.claim: The “reckoners” are angels who preserve and count human deeds.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p158#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p158#2/r7.speaker: مجاهد
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p158#2/r7.claim: Mujahid says the counters they tell to ask are the angels; Qatada says they mean people who calculate.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p158#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p158#2/r8.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p158#2/r8.claim: The wording does not specify angels or anyone else; it asks generally for whoever can count, since a sleeping or dead person does not measure time's passing.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p495/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p495/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p495/r1.claim: After witnessing the terrors and punishment, the people regard their stay as short; al-Farra says their answer means they do not know the actual duration.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p495/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p495/r2.speaker: مجاهد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p495/r2.claim: The العادين whom they are told to ask are angels.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p495/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p495/r3.speaker: قتادة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p495/r3.claim: Alternatively, العادين means those who count or keep account.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p495/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p495/r4.speaker: الحسن والزهري وأبو عمران الجوني وابن يعمر
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p495/r4.claim: They read العادين with a light, undoubled dāl.

RAZI-FULL:v23p110/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p110/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p110/r2.claim: The question is a rebuke: they denied any afterlife and imagined death as lasting extinction, so learning that Hell is eternal makes worldly life look brief and exposes their error.

RAZI-FULL:v23p110/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p110/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p110/r3.claim: They may have forgotten the duration amid terrors; their request to ask the counters signals that forgetfulness.

RAZI-FULL:v23p110/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p110/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v23p110/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says punishment made them forget what happened between the two blasts.

RAZI-FULL:v23p110/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p110/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p110/r5.claim: Alternatively, saying “a day or part of a day” minimizes their earthly stay beside the painful punishment they now know.

RAZI-FULL:v23p110/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p110/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p110/r6.claim: Some say the question concerns their lifespan in this world: God gave them time to know and act, but they answer that it was short despite having been told the world is brief.

RAZI-FULL:v23p110/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p110/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p110/r7.claim: Others say it concerns their stay after death; they argue that “in the earth” points to the grave, though the wording can also describe activity in the world.

RAZI-FULL:v23p110/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p110/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p110/r8.claim: The after-death view also appeals to criminals swearing they stayed no more than an hour, while believers say they remained until resurrection.

RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r1.speaker: منكرو عذاب القبر
RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r1.claim: Those denying grave punishment argue that if the dead were punished in their graves they would know their long stay and would not answer “a day or part of a day.”

RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r2.claim: The question may concern death with no life afterward until resurrection, a period that would include grave punishment.

RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r3.claim: Alternatively, it asks how long they were together, excluding some people's earlier deaths, so their perceived answer can still be a day or part of one.

RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r4.speaker: عكرمة
RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r4.claim: Ikrima takes “the counters” to mean the keepers who counted deeds, lifespans, and times of death.

RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r5.claim: Another explanation identifies the counters as angels who count the days and hours of worldly life.

RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r6.claim: They may instead mean: ask whoever knows the number, since they have forgotten it.

RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r7.claim: A lightened reading, al-ʿādīn, can mean unjust people, who would say the same thing.

RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p111/r8.claim: Another reading, al-ʿādiyīn, means the long-lived elders, who themselves consider their lives short.

QURTUBI-FULL:23:112-114/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:23:112-114/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:23:112-114/r3.claim: They may forget their time in the graves from the terror of punishment, or because torment was suspended between the two trumpet blasts; a comparison says those killed by or dying in a prophet’s presence are punished until the first blast, then held as still as water until the second.

QURTUBI-FULL:23:112-114/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:23:112-114/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:23:112-114/r4.claim: Another explanation is that they deem both worldly life and the grave interval brief beside what now faces them.

QURTUBI-FULL:23:112-114/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:23:112-114/r5.speaker: قتادة
QURTUBI-FULL:23:112-114/r5.claim: Qatadah says al-ʿāddīn are the people who count and know the duration; Mujahid says they are angels who were with people in the world.

BAYDAWI-FULL:23:113/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:23:113/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:23:113/r1.claim: They call their stay a day or part of one because it seems short beside eternal punishment, because happy days feel short, or because elapsed time is as nothing.

BAYDAWI-FULL:23:113/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:23:113/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:23:113/r2.claim: They tell the questioner to ask those able to count or angels who count lifespans and deeds; another light reading gives the sense of wrongdoers, and another means the ancients.

BAYDAWI-FULL:23:113/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:23:113/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:23:113/r3.claim: The phrase is also read al-ʿādīn for wrongdoers or al-ʿādiyīn for people of earlier generations.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p132#5/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p132#5/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p132#5/r1.claim: They underestimate worldly life relative to eternal punishment; people undergoing hardship experience time as long and days of ease as short.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p132#5/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p132#5/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p132#5/r2.claim: The counters may be arithmetic or angels who counted people's lifespans and deeds; the unhamzated “fasal” reading is Meccan and ʿAlī.

QASHANI:23:113-114/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:23:113-114/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
QASHANI:23:113-114/r1.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the people forget the interval of torment between the two trumpet blasts, during their concealment in the barzakh.

QASHANI:23:113-114/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:23:113-114/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:23:113-114/r2.claim: They call the stay brief because it has ended; God affirms it was brief, and knowing this would have led them to prepare and detach from its pleasures.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p588/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p588/r3.speaker: مجاهد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p588/r3.claim: Mujāhid identifies the counters as angels who record people's deeds and count their hours; Qatāda says they are accountants, while the author allows anyone who can count.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p588/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p588/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p588/r4.claim: The apparent sense includes angels or others who can count, since sleepers and the dead cannot track time. Al-Zamakhsharī says torment makes the interval feel slight and leaves them unable to calculate or explain it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p588/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p588/r5.speaker: الحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p588/r5.claim: Ḥasan and al-Kisāʾī transmit a light-dāl reading meaning wrongdoers; another form with long yāʾ means ancient people or long-lived elders, who would consider the period short too.

SAMIN-DURR:23:113/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:23:113/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:23:113/r1.claim: العادين in the common reading is the plural of عاد, a counter.

SAMIN-DURR:23:113/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:23:113/r2.speaker: الحسن والكسائي
SAMIN-DURR:23:113/r2.claim: A transmitted reading with light dāl makes العادين the plural active participle of عدا, meaning transgressors or oppressors.

SAMIN-DURR:23:113/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:23:113/r3.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:23:113/r3.claim: Abu al-Baqa takes the light-dāl reading as predecessors, like an old well; the author clarifies that the second, moving yāʾ is deleted first.

SAMIN-DURR:23:113/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:23:113/r4.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:23:113/r4.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reads العاديين as ancient long-lived people who would regard the reported duration as brief.

SAMIN-DURR:23:113/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:23:113/r5.speaker: ابن خالويه
SAMIN-DURR:23:113/r5.claim: Ibn Khalawayh notes a further form العاديين with a doubled yāʾ, the plural of عادية meaning the ancients.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p500/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p500/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p500/r1.claim: The question exposes how little of their short worldly lives they spent worshipping God; patience in that brief life would have brought the pious believers' success.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p500/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p500/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p500/r2.claim: They say they stayed a day or part of a day and are told to ask those who count the time.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p500/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p500/r4.speaker: أيفع بن عبد الكلاعي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p500/r4.claim: A report attributed to the Prophet says that, after the two groups enter their abodes, the people of Paradise call one brief day a good bargain for mercy and bliss, while the people of Hell made a bad bargain for fire and wrath.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p225#2/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p225#2/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p225#2/r4.claim: They answer that they stayed only a day or part of a day, minimizing worldly time beside the punishment and mistakenly supposing Hell's duration will match their earthly stay.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p225#2/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p225#2/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p225#2/r5.claim: Their appeal to the counters resembles worldly liars who ask someone else to authenticate their story; alternatively, they plead that torment has so occupied them they cannot recall or calculate the past.

DURR-FULL:v6p121/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p121/r1.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v6p121/r1.claim: Qatada interprets the ‘reckoners’ as those who count; Mujahid identifies them as angels.

BURSEVI:v6p78#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p78#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p78#2/r2.claim: They say a day or part of one because worldly life seems brief beside Hell's duration, because pleasurable days pass quickly, or because what is over is like nothing.

BURSEVI:v6p78#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p78#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p78#2/r3.claim: Those who could count their time say torment now occupies them so fully that they cannot remember or calculate it.

BURSEVI:v6p78#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p78#2/r4.speaker: التأويلات النجمية
BURSEVI:v6p78#2/r4.claim: The inward reading takes the counters as the angels assigned to record people's breaths, days, and nights.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p70/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p70/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p70/r1.claim: Their estimate of a day may minimize worldly residence compared with endless Hell; another view says worldly days seemed short because they were days of pleasure.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p70/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p70/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p70/r2.claim: A third view says elapsed time receives little attention, so they assume it was brief.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p70/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p70/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p70/r3.claim: Al-ʿĀddīn may be people capable of counting, since torment overwhelms them, or angels counting deeds, as reported from Mujāhid.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p70/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p70/r4.speaker: الحسن والكسائي
ALUSI-FULL:v18p70/r4.claim: A reading with light dāl means oppressors; followers supposedly called their leaders this for misleading them.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p70/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p70/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p70/r5.claim: A reading with doubled yāʾ relates the word to ʿĀd, famed for longevity, and means long-lived ancients who consider the stay brief.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p130#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p130#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p130#2/r4.claim: Their referral to the counters follows from uncertainty about the duration; Ibn ʿĀshūr suggests they invoke their worldly difficulty calculating years because of the nasīʾ calendar managed by Banū Kināna.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p130#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p130#2/r5.speaker: الكناني
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p130#2/r5.claim: The poet’s line about the nāsiʾūn of Maʿadd and making months forbidden witnesses to the calendar intercalation practice.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p130#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p130#2/r6.speaker: المفسرون
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p130#2/r6.claim: Other commentators take the counters to be angels or people who remember the duration; al-Qurṭubī says to ask the calculators who know because the speakers forgot.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p131/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p131/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p131/r4.claim: Their answer shows they know they were underground but cannot recall the duration; they estimate a day or part of one by familiar earthly days, as in 30:55.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p131/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p131/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p131/r5.claim: The question and answer indirectly prove they emerged alive from earth, refuting their denial and their claim that life cannot return to bones and remains after centuries.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p131/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p131/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p131/r6.claim: God makes them state that the stay seemed short to magnify their error: restored bodies and thought lead them to suppose little time passed, compounding their false premise.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p132/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p132/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p132/r1.claim: Their request to ask the counters admits they cannot measure the stay; they imagine the world still continues and disclaim responsibility for an imprecise answer.

TABATABAI:23:99-118#4/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:23:99-118#4/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:23:99-118#4/r2.claim: They answer that they stayed a day or part of one earthly day because, beside eternal life now visible to them, their grave stay seems brief; other verses estimate an hour or part of a day.

TABATABAI:23:99-118#4/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:23:99-118#4/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:23:99-118#4/r3.claim: “Ask the counters” means they cannot count the duration accurately and should ask those who counted; these may be the angels who count the days.

TABATABAI:23:99-118#6/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:23:99-118#6/r7.speaker: الملائكة
TABATABAI:23:99-118#6/r7.claim: Al-Qummi glosses “ask the counters” as asking angels who count days and record the hours and deeds people acquire.

ASAD-NOTES:23:112#n66/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:23:112#n66/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:23:112#n66/r1.claim: The allegorical exchange presents human time as illusory and worldly life as negligible beside the ultimate, perhaps timeless reality known to God.

ASAD-NOTES:23:112#n66/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:23:112#n66/r2.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:23:112#n66/r2.claim: The reply to ask those who count signals that resurrection removes humanity's earthbound sense of time.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p279/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p279/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p279/r1.claim: Rejecters will discover that the respite they thought long passed in a blink; they will then deeply regret their conduct.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p284/r6.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p284/r6.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p284/r6.claim: The delay in resurrection will soon be exposed as a misconception: what people imagined to be a long earthly life will end like a blink.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p284/r9.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p284/r9.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p284/r9.claim: The respondents' direction to ask those who counted expresses their aversion to a question about the life whose imagined length had enamored them.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p285/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p285/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p285/r1.claim: The dialogue about earthly life occurs among the people themselves, as the parallel exchange in Ṭāhā makes explicit.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p285/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p285/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p285/r2.claim: The dialogue in the Cave sūrah likewise shows people speaking among themselves; it exemplifies awakening from sleep in Barzakh.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:112/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:112/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:112/r1.claim: The afterlife dialogue is representative: earthly time is a perception shaped by worldly conditions, and passage into eternal life changes one’s sense of time.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:112/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:112/r2.speaker: tefsirler
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:23:112/r2.claim: Commentators identify those charged with counting as either angels or people engaged in reckoning.

QIRAAT-ER:23:113:8#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:23:113:8#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:23:113:8#1/r1.claim: Eliding hamza from saʾala to sala is a common Hijazi or Meccan phonological simplification without semantic change.

STUDYQURAN:23:112/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:23:112/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:23:112/r1.claim: The Hereafter makes people view their whole worldly life as no more than a day or hour.

STUDYQURAN:23:intro/r10.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:23:intro/r10.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:23:intro/r10.claim: The grandeur of the Hereafter makes worldly life seem like a day or part of a day.

STUDYQURAN:23:intro/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:23:intro/r7.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:23:intro/r7.claim: The opposition of affluent and powerful people to prophets recurs throughout this surah, as elsewhere in the Quran.

STUDYQURAN:23:intro/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:23:intro/r9.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:23:intro/r9.claim: The conclusion warns that disbelievers facing their perdition will wish to return to do good instead of evil, but it will be too late.
